name: Union of Concerned Scientists: food and farms (charityevals)
summary: The Union of Concerned Scientists' Food and Environment programme ($4.5M in the year to September 2025, $5.1M with overhead) does analysis and advocacy on farms and food: wetlands and the farm bill's conservation rules, fertilizer, groundwater, farm trade and farmworkers. This model counts its one win of the year with a value at stake: its estimate that the Upper Midwest's wetlands avert about $23 billion of flood damage a year helped defend the federal wetland protections (Swampbuster) against a 2025 challenge that could have struck them down; its other work is a share. At the defaults a dollar given keeps about 0.004 years of healthy life per $1,000 (flood damage averted, valued as consumption to the average American), from 0.0001 to 0.11 on the combined range. It is small because the challenge was unlikely to succeed, the government and other groups did most of the defence (UCS is credited with 3%), and the money kept goes to US households, where a dollar does far less than in poor countries. The result is mostly uncertainty: the share credited to UCS, the share of wetlands that would be drained and the chance the challenge would have won each move it about ten times. The one branch is discounted for missing data: nothing about the work's outcome is measured.

source.title: DTN Progressive Farmer (5 December 2024), Union of Concerned Scientists calls for wetland protections in farm bill
source.quote: this flood protection equates to nearly $23 billion in annual residential flood protection
source.note: UCS's analysis of the Upper Midwest's 30 million acres of wetlands (its annual report, p. 15: 'they prevent almost $23 billion in flood damage every year'). The range is ours: one study's model of residential flood losses, so -35% to +30%.

rows.explainer: UCS's own estimate (December 2024) of the residential flood damage the Upper Midwest's wetlands avert each year: nearly $23 billion ($15 to $30 billion, our range around one study's figure). It is the value at stake when federal wetland protections are challenged.

rows.label: Share of that flood protection lost over the years counted if the protections fell
rows.explainer: Swampbuster (1985) denies farm subsidies to farmers who drain wetlands on their land; Sodbuster does the same for highly erodible land. Had the challenge struck them down, part of the region's farmed wetlands would be drained over the following years (the region lost most of its wetlands to drainage before 1985). An average 5% of the protection lost over the years counted (1% to 15%), our judgment: about 1-2% of the wetlands drained a year, accumulating, on the share of them on farmland.

source.title: Iowa Environmental Council (29 May 2025), Victory: judge rules against dangerous case seeking to gut wetland protections
source.quote: the program could have been revoked entirely, along with its sister program, Sodbuster

rows.label: Value of a dollar of flood damage averted to US households, in units of value
rows.explainer: A dollar of flood damage averted, valued like a dollar of consumption to the average American: one over consumption per person (2024, in 2025 dollars) in ln(consumption), × the shared value of doubling consumption, as the Federation of American Scientists' model values a dollar of US public good.

rows.label: Value kept per dollar of the yearly protection, in units of value
Chance the challenge would in the end have struck down the protections
rows.explainer: CTM Holdings v. USDA argued that Swampbuster exceeds Congress's power and aimed for the Supreme Court; earlier challenges all failed, but the Supreme Court has narrowed federal wetland power before (Sackett v. EPA, 2023). One event, so drawn as one: 10% (2% to 30%), our judgment.

rows.label: Years a won reform counts before it would have come anyway
rows.explainer: The shared years a won reform counts ($win_years_counted): the protections kept count for the years before the question would have been settled anyway.

rows.label: Years from the win until the policy takes effect
rows.explainer: Had the challenge succeeded (a ruling in 2025, appeals after), drainage would follow within about a year or two: 1 (0 to 3), our judgment; discounted at the shared rate.

rows.label: Discount for the wait until the policy takes effect
rows.explainer: The wait discounted at the shared rate.

rows.label: Discounted years of impact
rows.explainer: The years counted, discounted, after the wait.

rows.label: Flood protection kept over the years counted, in units of value (before adjustments)
rows.explainer: The yearly protection × the share at stake × its value per dollar × the chance the challenge would have succeeded × the discounted years.

rows.label: Evidence adjustment (internal and external validity), a multiplier
rows.explainer: The $23 billion is UCS's own model of residential flood losses, not peer-reviewed evaluation, and the share drained without the protections is a judgment: 0.7 (0.4 to 1.0), our judgment, as the template's default for a single study.

rows.label: Share of that chance the 2025 ruling removed
rows.explainer: The district court's ruling (29 May 2025, Northern District of Iowa) kept the protections, but it can be appealed, and the government defends them too: half the chance of their falling removed by the ruling, 0.5 (0.2 to 0.8), our judgment.

rows.label: UCS's share of the resources behind the defence
rows.explainer: The defence was the Justice Department's for USDA and the intervenors' (the Iowa Farmers Union, the Iowa Environmental Council, Dakota Rural Action and Food & Water Watch, represented by the Environmental Law & Policy Center); UCS's wetland analysis is cited in the case's background and its annual report says it 'helped defeat' the lawsuit (p. 15). UCS's share of all resources behind the win, 3% (0.5% to 10%), our judgment.

source.title: Union of Concerned Scientists, 2025 Annual Report (fiscal year 1 October 2024 to 30 September 2025)
source.quote: it helped defeat a lawsuit that could have gutted longstanding federal protections

rows.label: Share of credit used
rows.explainer: The charity's share of the resources behind the outcome; it applies whichever way credit is shared.

rows.label: Counted less where the outcome isn't measured for this charity
rows.explainer: Thin: no outcome of the work is measured (the protection kept is UCS's own estimate and the chances are judged), so the shared missing-data step applies (docs/normalization.md 2.12).

rows.label: All adjustments combined
rows.explainer: The product of the adjustments above.

rows.label: Other food and farm work, as a share of the modelled value
rows.explainer: The rest of the programme, each part a share of the wetland branch's value: fertilizer (nitrogen) analysis and advocacy, whose cuts in nitrous oxide and nitrate pollution would count in tonnes and health; the San Joaquin Valley groundwater recommendations; the farm bill's conservation programmes and farmworkers' heat and pesticide protections; analysis of the costs of tariffs to farmers. None has a counted win of the year, so each counts only for the chance it moves a later rule: together half the wetland branch's value, 50% (15% to 60%), our judgment, inside the family's bounds; the climate part of the fertilizer work would be worth more if a rule followed.
